subject: Secure external access recommendation for Lighthouse Analytics - options and MAP
messages:
From: Alex Turner <alex.turner@lighthouse.ai>
To: Ben Carter <ben.carter@redwood.ai>
Cc: 
Date: Thu, 05 Mar 2026 09:12:00 -0700
Subject: Quick question — private deploy connectivity options

Ben —

Thanks again for the demo last week. We’re evaluating Redwood Private for inference in our AWS accounts + an on-prem datacenter. Before we start procurement we need your recommendation on connectivity patterns: VPC peering, PrivateLink (endpoint services), or a site-to-site VPN into our VPC/Transit Gateway.

Constraints that matter to us:
- We need predictable egress IPs to allowlist with partners.
- No cross-account routing that exposes our internal VPCs to third parties.
- On-prem traffic for certain workloads (PHI) needs to stay private.
- Minimal networking ops overhead is preferred — our NetOps team is small.

Can you outline trade-offs and a recommended approach for Lighthouse? Specific ask: one-page summary + proposed next steps for a pilot.

— Alex
Alex Turner
Head of Platform, Lighthouse Analytics
alex.turner@lighthouse.ai
From: Ben Carter <ben.carter@redwood.ai>
To: Alex Turner <alex.turner@lighthouse.ai>
Cc: Karthik Iyer <karthik.iyer@redwood.ai>, Marissa Cole <marissa.cole@redwood.ai>
Date: Thu, 05 Mar 2026 11:03:00 -0700
Subject: Re: Quick question — private deploy connectivity options

Alex —

Short answer up front: for Lighthouse’s constraints I recommend PrivateLink (AWS interface endpoints / endpoint service) as the primary pattern, with a site-to-site VPN to your on-prem as an optional parallel path for workloads that must remain entirely within your datacenter.

Why PrivateLink first:
- No cross-account route propagation: PrivateLink terminates at VPC endpoints you control, so we don’t require peering or exposing our routing tables to your VPCs.
- Static endpoint ENIs -> predictable private IPs for allowlists inside your VPC (and we can publish egress NAT IPs if you use an egress appliance).
- Strong security boundary: TLS + mTLS between client and endpoint is straightforward, and we can support VPC endpoint policy scoping.

When peering helps:
- If you have extremely latency-sensitive traffic and both sides are in the same AWS region/account boundary, VPC peering yields slightly lower RTTs and avoids ENI hop, but it requires careful CIDR planning and you cannot use transitive peering.

When VPN makes sense:
- For on-prem integration and if you require a single managed public IP for egress, S2S (or Transit Gateway S2S) is a practical fallback. It’s operationally simpler for small NetOps teams but can add latency and needs encryption/MTU tuning.

Next steps I propose:
1) We validate which AWS accounts/VPCs you want to expose to Redwood and collect CIDRs.
2) We provide a PrivateLink config checklist (we’ll attach).
3) Optional: schedule a 60-min network kickoff with NetOps to agree on CIDRs, endpoint policies, and test window.

I attached a short PrivateLink checklist with key configuration items and limits (attachment: privatelink-config-checklist.xlsx). Karthik and Marissa are cc’d to add technical and rollout details.

If you prefer, we can also map a hybrid approach: PrivateLink + Transit Gateway S2S for on-prem PHI flows.

Best,
Ben

Subject: Re: Quick question — private deploy connectivity options

Alex, Ben —

Adding a few engineering bullets to supplement Ben’s notes:
- AWS limits: interface endpoints create ENIs in subnets — watch AZ coverage and endpoint ENI IP usage. If you have /28 subnets in the endpoint subnets you may exhaust addresses quickly.
- Route tables: PrivateLink does not require route table entries in the same way peering does; avoids transitive clutter.
- DNS: we push a private DNS name (svc.redwood-inference.internal) — ensure your resolver forwards correctly from on-prem if you need on-prem -> PrivateLink.
- MTU / fragmentation: S2S VPNs often need MTU tuning for gso/gro on large payloads. Test with real payloads.
- Egress allowlisting: PrivateLink keeps traffic inside the cloud, but if you need a single public egress IP for partner allowlist, consider adding NAT through a controlled egress firewall in your VPC or use a static IP egress appliance.
- Performance: our internal tests show PrivateLink adds ~1–3ms above peering in-region for small requests; for token-heavy streaming workloads the delta is usually dominated by model runtime, not the extra hop.
- Failure modes: with peering a routing mistake can expose routes; PrivateLink reduces blast radius because you control which subnets host endpoints and can limit endpoint policy.

If you can share the candidate VPC CIDRs and whether you want endpoints wired into a private subnet with NAT, I’ll draft a short network test plan (iperf + small token streaming) to validate latency and MTU.

-Karthik
Karthik Iyer
Solutions Architect — Redwood Inference

Thanks Ben / Karthik —

A couple clarifications from our side after talking to NetOps:
- We cannot accept VPC peering that requires route propagation from outside vendors; our security policy forbids cross-account route injection.
- We do need a predictable set of egress IPs for a handful of external partners (they only allow IP-based ACLs).
- On-prem traffic must remain within our datacenter for PHI workloads; those teams want an audited VPN path.

Given that, PrivateLink as the primary ingress + Transit Gateway S2S from on-prem sounds closest to what we need. Could you put together a recommended configuration that includes:
1) endpoint service + interface endpoint design (subnet sizing, AZs)
2) where we would terminate TLS/mTLS and cert exchange process
3) how to provide a stable egress IP set (NAT or egress appliance options)
4) test plan and estimated timeline for a 3-week pilot

NetOps — I’ve looped you in so we can share CIDRs and schedule the kickoff.

— Alex

Subject: Re: Quick question — private deploy connectivity options

Alex / NetOps —

Thanks — below is a concise mutual action plan (MAP) and recommended config for the Lighthouse pilot. I’ve attached a simple network diagram showing Endpoint placement (attachment: lh-network-diagram.pdf).

MAP (3-week pilot):
Week 0 — Kickoff (collect VPC IDs, CIDRs, NetOps contact; agree on test window)
Week 1 — PrivateLink endpoint service established in Redwood account; Lighthouse creates interface endpoints in nominated VPC subnets (we’ll provide Terraform snippets).
Week 2 — Run network tests (iperf + token streaming), validate TLS/mTLS handshake, and exercise cert rotation.
Week 3 — Exercise egress path: we’ll demo a small NAT egress appliance option that publishes a static IP set for partner allowlists. If needed, enable Transit Gateway S2S to route PHI flows to on-prem.

Recommended config notes:
- Endpoint AZ coverage: create endpoints in at least 2 AZs (3 preferred) and reserve /26 per AZ for ENIs if you have many endpoints or scale concerns.
- Endpoint policies: restrict to the specific VPC principals and tie to service name.
- TLS termination: we recommend mutual TLS where Redwood validates client certs; cert exchange via shared CA or pre-provisioned client certs.
- Egress: simplest path is a small NAT instance/Cluster with Elastic IPs (we can prototype). For production we recommend an HA NAT/egress appliance behind an NLB so you get consistent public IPs.

To proceed I need:
- NetOps contact for scheduling the kickoff (email + preferred times)
- VPC IDs and CIDR blocks for the VPCs where you’ll place interface endpoints
- Any existing NAT/ePy appliances you want us to integrate with

If NetOps is OK with the plan we’ll schedule a 60-minute kickoff — I’ll bring the PrivateLink Terraform + test plan.

— Marissa
